John Legend and Bobby Cannavale are among the guest stars in the second season, which finds Ansari’s put-upon actor, Dev, returning to New York after a brief sojourn in Italy.—
After their reckless handling of a “Minotaur” energy drink truck, two knuckleheads (Paul Rudd and Seann William Scott) are sentenced to 150 hours of community service, during which time they serve as Big Brothers for a pair of troubled kids (Bobb’e J. Thompson and Christopher Mintz-Plasse). It may sound like a sappy redemption comedy, but the director David Wain, working with many of his ensemble-mates from “The State” and “Wet Hot American Summer,” turns “Role Models” into a foul-mouthed, emphatically offensive delight.—
The notion of a sequel to Steven Soderbergh’ssleeper hitabout male strippers in a Tampa nightclub may sound thinner than a thong, but “Magic Mike XXL” is bigger and perhaps better than its predecessor. On top of one thrilling dance sequence after another, from Channing Tatum’s welding and grinding to Ginuwine’s “Pony” to Joe Manganiello’s impromptu convenience store jam to the Backstreet Boys, the film’s road-movie spontaneity allows for the unexpected and brings the most out of the ensemble.—
Covering three stages in the life of an alienated and sexually confused kid in the Miami projects, Barry Jenkins’s Oscar-winning drama deals poignantly with a boy’s sublimated desires in a culture that forbids their expression. All three parts feature different actors and textures, but they’re united by Jenkins’ deep compassion for his characters, a superb ensemble cast and a heightened, poetic style that recalls Terrence Malick and Wong Kar-wai.—
Mental illness has been a hidden theme of David O. Russell comedies like “Spanking the Money,” “Flirting with Disaster,” and “I Heart Huckabees,” but “Silver Linings Playbook” finally makes it explicit, staging a romantic comedy on a Tilt-a-Whirl of manic-depression. Bradley Cooper and Jennifer Lawrence have excellent chemistry as two emotionally fragile people who take some refuge in each other, and Robert De Niro is more committed than usual as a father whose Philadelphia Eagles obsession masks true heartbreak and concern over his son’s unraveling.—
Neither movies about the zombie apocalypse nor movies about young, Chosen One types are in short supply right now, but “The Girl with All the Gifts” combines the two into a compelling hybrid that’s greater than the sum of its parts. With humankind decimated by a disease that turns victims into “hungries,” there is a handful of immune children who are subjected to government tests, including a little girl who may hold the key to survival. “The Girl With All the Gifts” delivers the requisite flesh-gnawing action, but it’s thoughtful about humanity’s place on the earth and whether it’s worthy of redemption.—

The trial of a Queens man charged in the fatal shooting of the New York City police officer Brian Moore ended on Wednesday with the two sides painting bitterly opposite views of the defendant and the circumstances of the shooting more than two years ago.
A lawyer for Demetrius Blackwell, the accused man, argued that his client who has struggled for years with seizures from severe epilepsy had been wrongly identified as Officer Moore’s assailant. For nearly two hours, he attacked the credibility of the prosecution’s prime witnesses.
“This is the kind of stuff that reasonable doubt is made out of,” the lawyer David A. Bart said.
Daniel Saunders, an assistant district attorney, countered that the shooting on a residential block in Queens Village in May 2015 was a calculated burst of violence by an antisocial career criminal. Mr. Saunders said Mr. Blackwell’s DNA was found on a bullet cartridge in the weapon used in the shooting, a five-shot revolver that was found in a backyard two days after the encounter with two bullets still in its cylinder.
After the closing arguments in State Supreme Court in Queens, the jury began deliberations, which are scheduled to resume on Thursday.
